utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01554, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you, in the course of 1998 and 1999, hear of an organisation or a group that was referred to as a Black Hand?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the question, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of the group. There were rumours, comments were made, extensive comments, though that group was formed by so-called KLA members apparently. And in the evening hours and early morning hours it was said that they would drive around in civilian cars and engage in acts of murder and looting. I've heard of such a KLA organisation. Both Serbs and Albanians commented on this. Such was the information, the operative information we had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This Court has heard evidence from one Bedri Hyseni. Do you know this person, Bedri Hyseni; does that name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name and surname ring a bell, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He was -- is a human rights activist for an organisation called the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedom, and he was also a law professor in Kosovo. Does that help you to remember him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now it's a little clearer for me, but I still can't remember what the person looked like. But I believe that there was such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you hear of the Council for Defence of Human Rights and Freedom? Or did you know of its work?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I had heard of it. But as of its work, I didn't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, they would issue press releases from time to time about human rights conditions in Kosovo and in Urosevac in particular. Did you know of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember such things, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Hyseni testified that the actions of the Black Hand, including killings, were aimed at the Kosovo Albanian population. Do you recall Kosovo Albanians being victims of this so-called Black Hand?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the victims, the Serbians, the Albanians, and everyone were the victims if they didn't agree with their plan, with their strategy, with the KLA strategy. I'm not aware of the existence of some other Black Hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I think that is where the real difference is. He said that they would go around mainly at night in private cars and commit atrocities, but he is saying that they were committing atrocities primarily against Kosovo Albanians and that they would act in concert with the police. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I don't think that's correct. You know, a lot of propaganda was spread by Albanians with regard to various issues. I don't want to speak about history here, but the purpose was separatism, to have a Kosovo secede. So it was necessary to spread such propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you know of a policemen in Urosevac that they called Pokran or Pucran?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That name means nothing to me, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You know of a policeman with that name who had a BMW motor vehicle?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A policeman driving a BMW? Well that was quite rare. The salaries were such that it was impossible to even drive around in a little Fiat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's why I hoped that you would remember him. Hyseni testified that a policeman named Pukran, known to be very aggressive and crude towards the Kosovo Albanian population at the check-points, would allow his BMW to be used by the Black Hand. This is 4915 of the transcript. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I've never heard of this name. I don't know. I've never heard of a policeman by that name. But on the whole, I knew all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Hyseni testified at 4889 of the transcript that on one occasion - this would be sometime in 1998 or early 1999 - there were two young men who were killed by the Black Hand, two Albanian young men, and this was not even reported to the police because, and I quote him, and he is speaking of the Urosevac police station at that time: "If you went to the police station at that time, you were hardly likely to come out alive from there." This may be a flowery language, but were you aware that by the time of the NATO intervention, Kosovo Albanians, especially those who are involved in any political action that you might call separatist, were so terrorised and persecuted by the police that many of them feared going to the police station?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This isn't true. The claim that they couldn't even go to the police station whenever they had matters of interest to deal with, they went to the police station. Saying that they couldn't go is propaganda. And let me tell you another thing. Through the media, I heard of certain individuals who had even been killed. Mehme [phoen] Agani, I believe that's the name, but the perpetrator was found and processed. I think this was in Kosovo Polje, somewhere around there. I read that in the press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think we have to leave that there and move on to another topic, Mr. Mitic. Before I do, I'm reminded that the document marked P5053 should be received under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you mean P1553?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be under seal. Are you moving on now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Oh, I -- it might well be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the second break and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Mitic, you told us earlier about the sincerity of Mr. Janicevic. Are you aware that he attended this Tribunal and testified in another case in 2005?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of that, but I don't know the details because I didn't follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, right throughout your testimony, mainly in chief, you gave us a lot of evidence which was based on information you received from him, and I take it you relied upon information that you received from him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I relied on that information because he was a chief of the secretariat, and he familiarised us with dispatches and other documents at meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like you to comment on certain aspects of what he said when he testified here under solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could look at the transcript of the Milosevic trial, 4th of October, 2005, at page 41153. I think we uploaded it into e-court at 6068, but it is part of the records of this Tribunal, so it should be available. 45153, if we could try to find that page. Oh, it appears that the numbers in e-court might not be ... they might not correspond to the numbers on the document. It's page 58 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And let me read to you what the SUP chief Janicevic said: "I think it was on the 12th of January. Prior to that, operative intelligence was sent to the MUP staff in Pristina about the events taking place in Stimlje municipality on the axis toward Dulje, in the Crnoljevo gorge, and on the Pristina-Urosevac road. "On the 12th, at my briefing with my commanders, I agree that we would make a draft plan for an anti-terrorist action to be submitted to the staff in Urosevac because we knew by that time that there was a large terrorist group of about 80 men headed by Afet Bilalli, nickname Qopa, who was mounting daily attacks on the road, targeting anything that moves. They were kidnapping innocent people, stopping traffic, attacking the police and the convoys. The last in the series of attacks was the attack on Slivovo village where policeman Przic was killed. I sent this plan to Pristina, to the MUP staff." Is this, what I just read, true to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was roughly that way. Around the 12th, Mr. Janicevic, the chief of the secretariat, drafted his suggestion. But with regard to the intelligence and everything else, I believe he made a security assessment, as far as I remember, and that was the assessment of the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Following that, he testified that: "When I arrived at the staff, I presented this plan in the presence of staff commander Lukic and the head of the department Vlastimir Djordjevic. I told them about everything that was going on. They had known some of this information from before. They looked at the plan, and they accepted it." Firstly, were you aware that he presented the plan to Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that the plan had been taken to the staff, and we got feedback that the staff had approved the plan. Or rather, that the -- that a plan would be worked out at staff level --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for the purpose of apprehending the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We are talking about people here. Mr. Lukic was head of the staff. He says he presented the plan in the presence of the head of the staff, Lukic, and the head of the department, Mr. Djordjevic. Firstly, did you become aware that he presented a plan to the -- to General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief didn't tell us at the meeting, nor did I hear it from anybody else except --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you become aware -- did you become aware that he also presented the plan to General Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard of General Djordjevic being acquainted with this plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you aware that both Lukic and Mr. Djordjevic were aware of much of the intelligence in respect to what was happening in Stimlje? And this is about the 12th of January.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that General Lukic was aware. I'm sure that he monitored the situation. But I don't know about General Djordjevic. We weren't, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, you don't know about Mr. Djordjevic. That's an answer. This is what Mr. Janicevic testified to under solemn declaration here. Do you have any reason that you can offer why Mr. Janicevic would be lying about these matters?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that he wouldn't be lying. He probably mixed up the dates or possibly his memory isn't reliable enough, because he had family problems and many other problems. I believe that he couldn't remember all details. And possibly it was due to carelessness that he gave such a statement and not because he intentionally wanted to lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So your -- very well. That is your explanation. He said, further: "Goran Radosavljevic, as staff member, was appointed to lead this action. The action was agreed to take place on the 13th; however, on the 13th, it was not carried out because the weather did not allow it. It was too cold and there were other problems as well. We postponed it until the 15th."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of this situation, namely the fact that the operation was delayed. Nobody informed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He goes on: "On the 14th, in the evening, at the office of the head of the SUP, that's where I was, in addition to company commander, the chief of the police station was invited, Goran Radosavljevic as well, as well as the leader of the Operative Pursuit Group and platoon commanders, and Colonel" - and there was an interruption - "who was also invited to acquaint himself with this plan. There was no signing. Nobody signed. Radosavljevic; Colonel Krsman, Jelic; or anybody else." So I think what Mr. Janicevic was saying - it seems quite clear here - that Colonel Jelic was also invited to acquaint himself with this plan. I think that is your testimony. Does this, which I read, accord with your memory? Is it substantively correct -- substantially correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know something, last time I also emphasised that I was summoned by the chief on the 14th in the evening. The chief of the SUP was there; then the commander of the PJP company Lecic; then Goran Radosavljevic, who headed the OPG on the following day; and Krsman Jelic was invited later because he was to be informed only. The administration building of the military was just across the road. We were neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but it sounds to me that you agree with what I just read of the testimony of Mr. Janicevic, Bogoljub Janicevic, is substantially correct. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What precisely do you mean, because you asked a lot of questions so could you be more precise. What do you want me to confirm?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you already have. There was this meeting on the 14th with the company commanders, yourself, the chief of the police station, Goran Radosavljevic, and Colonel Jelic? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The company commander, one man, not several. Not company commanders, just one company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the rest is substantially correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So: "The plan was only approved, and the approval process is done on the map including the participation of the head of department because all the preconditions had been created for mounting this anti-terrorist operation and for eliminating this terrorist group that had already wielded a lot of evil in the area." He's saying, essentially, that they -- there needed to be no agreement or signing in this meeting because a plan had been approved already by the head of the department which -- who is General Djordjevic, again repeating the same thing he said earlier. Is Mr. Janicevic -- was he being untruthful, or was he a man that you rely upon to speak the truth?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that not even on that evening was General Djordjevic mentioned. He merely explained to us that the plan had been approved at the level of the staff and that the operation was to take place on the following day. He gave that information to Colonel Jelic because he needed to know because of his people. He was the commander of that area and had to be informed of a police operation taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If we could move to page 41 -- sorry, page 45157. I think that's two -- about two or three pages further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In this section, Mr. Geoffrey Nice is asking Mr. Janicevic questions on the basis of a statement given by Mr. Radosavljevic, and from lines 8 he is quoting a question to Mr. Radosavljevic. And this is in respect to the events of the 15th of January. "General Djordjevic was close to the scene, was he in a police station or a command post?" And Radosavljevic said: "I later heard he was in the police station. I met him at night, in the evening." Then Radosavljevic was asked: "Which police station was that?" The answer: "The police station in Stimlje, which was the closest police station." Then Mr. Nice goes further down -- a couple of questions further down in Radosavljevic's statement -- or question/answer: "Q. General Lukic was in the immediate area of the operation ...?" "A. I think he was in the staff, because I talked to him through the radio a few times." That was the answer of Mr. Radosavljevic. And then Mr. Nice asked Mr. Janicevic: "Do you agree with all that about Mr. Djordjevic and Lukic?" And Janicevic said: "Lukic was at the staff and Djordjevic was at the staff too." Were you aware that that day, the 15th, both Mr. Lukic and Mr. Djordjevic were at the staff in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Then Mr. Nice asked: "And at the police station --" And Mr. Janicevic said: "But -- may I just explain, please. At 1100, Djordjevic came to the police station in Stimlje with his driver. He came to make inquiries, to find out how the operation was coming along, and at 11.30 he left for Pristina. Therefore, Goran Radosavljevic had not the slightest chance to meet him at the police station in Stimlje. General Djordjevic spent about 30 minutes at the police station all in all." "What about contacts with --" And the answer of General -- of Mr. Janicevic is: "He didn't even sit down." Mr. Janicevic is here saying - and let's not quibble about the time. He says 11.00, but the central piece of this is that General Djordjevic came there that morning, the 15th. Do you agree with Mr. Janicevic's evidence on this point? Did you know that he came there that morning?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I remember the 18th when we carried out an on-site investigation --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 15th, did you know that he was there on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I can claim with full responsibility that I didn't see General Djordjevic there on the 15th. And, again, I'm saying that perhaps Janicevic confused the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, he might have made a mistake with the time, but you see that he is not just speaking about a date, he is speaking about a context. He is giving evidence about how the operation was planned and it developed. So a mistake in terms of numbers and dates doesn't arise here, Mr. Mitic. Let me ask you this -- or let me put it to you that Mr. Janicevic, your chief, testified to the truth when said that Mr. Djordjevic went to Stimlje the morning of the operation.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he is right. I remember very well -- well, to be frank, I didn't see General Djordjevic very often, but I remember this very well because I was ordered to carry out this on-site investigation on behalf of the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, my next suggestion is that General Djordjevic was there in your presence, he was in a room present with you and the SUP chief Mr. Janicevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was, but on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the 15th, my suggestion is, at the onset of this operation, he was present in the room with yourself and Mr. Janicevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, my memory still serves me well. I remember this very well. And I'm telling you the reason for which I can remember this, it's because the SUP chief in the presence of the general ordered me to take an on-site investigation team to Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you speak about memory. Would you agree with me that General Djordjevic -- would you agree with me that Mr. Janicevic's memory in October 2005 would be fresher in respect to these events than your memory now? I withdraw that. That's a rhetorical question. If we could move on. From line 6, the question was: "What about contacts with or did you make phone calls to Mr. Sainovic or did --" To which Mr. Janicevic responded: "What contact?" And Mr. Nice said after that: "Were there phone calls made to Mr. Sainovic from your police station?" And he responded: "I have never spoken to Sainovic in my life." Question: "Were you aware of his speaking to anybody else at your police station?" To which Mr. Janicevic responded: "Nobody from the police station, no. No, not from the police station." You remember Mr. Maisonneuve had said that Mr. Janicevic was erudite and sometimes could - and I'm para-phrasing him - could evade a question, you needed to press him. Well, we see here he is being asked about Mr. Sainovic speaking to somebody at the police station, and he answers twice, making a distinction to somebody from the police station. Well, I'd like to ask you to search your memory. Can you remember that a call came to Mr. Sainovic -- sorry, a call came into Mr. Djordjevic, not one, two calls, from Mr. Sainovic on the morning when he was at the police station?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Let me repeat this. On the 18th, when General Djordjevic came to Stimlje, the SUP chief, myself, and Danica Marinkovic, the investigative judge were present. Then there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, there is really no need to repeat it. I've heard it more than once. I --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only wanted to say that at that time between the 15 or 20 minutes that we spent there together, well, I went to Racak with this on-site investigation team. And after that, I don't know whether he had contact with anyone. But that wasn't the case while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, when you left to go to Racak, did you leave Mr. Djordjevic in the office?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In any case, you are saying, I suppose, that it is possible that something might have happened after you left, but my suggestion to you, again, is that Mr. Djordjevic was there on the morning of the 15th while the operation was on-going.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as my memory serves me, I remember this very well, and I have given you the reason. On the 15th, he wasn't there. But the 18th is more interesting for publicity and so on and so forth. So that's why I assume the ministry sent him. And I was there on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, in his testimony on the 30th of September, 2005, in the Milosevic case at page 44906 of the record, I wonder if we could have a look at that very briefly.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only have the English version. I don't have the other version on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll read it to you and I'll try to read it slowly, so if you could listen carefully. Yes, at this point, Judge Kwon said: "We've had enough, so why don't you go straight to 15 January." And again, it's the third time, Mr. Janicevic -- the question is asked: "Let's clear this up. You just mentioned this plan. That plan was approve. Who approved it?" And Mr. Janicevic said: "Chief of sector, Vlastimir Djordjevic." For the third time - I just want you to focus - this is the third occasion that Mr. Janicevic testified to this. Can't you recall becoming aware that the approval procedure involved Mr. Djordjevic? He was, in fact, the chief.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, by no means. I'm quite convinced that the staff took the decision, drew up a plan, and General Djordjevic, well, perhaps he was subsequently familiarised with this, but he didn't take any decisions with regard to this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He was also asked: "How many policemen were engaged in the implementation of the operation, from your secretariat and from the staff?" And his response was: "One hundred and five members of the Special Police Unit and 30 members of the Operation Pursuit Group." And the next question: "The 105 members were from your secretariat and you are their immediate superior?" And the answer was: "Yes." Those two answers that Mr. Janicevic gave, are they substantially correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were 105 members, that's the Urosevac company strength. I am not sure about these 30 men; I don't know whether the figure was higher perhaps for these members of the special group. As far as the Special Police Unit is concerned, the chief of the secretariat couldn't have led that unit. Perhaps he believed that they were his men, his employees, but as for him directly leading that special unit, no, not even in a dream, because they have their own chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But they were employees of his SUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were SUP employees. So perhaps that's why he counted them as his own men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If it would please Your Honours, I would like to tender those passages from Mr. Janicevic's testimony and ask that they be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received. Mr. Djurdjic, I see you standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think it should be done under the same conditions that were applied to similar statements. It should be marked for identification; and if so, then I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you I may, Your Honour, with respect, this now is an entirely different situation. While I concede that counsel might have been right in respect to the earlier statements the witness was shown, in this case, this is a witness of -- this is a statement of a chief of a SUP. And before -- I don't think I need to remind the Court that the hearsay would be admissible before the Tribunal depending on the reliability. The important thing is that in this case it was the Defence that opened the door to the reliability of the statement. In chief, they asked the witness to testify to a variety of matters that the witness could only testify to on the basis of what Mr. Janicevic said. And that's why it's an important reason why this is different, because the Defence has opened the door to the admissibility of Mr. Janicevic's statements. And the other thing is that this is a sworn statement given before the Tribunal, so it is manifestly reliable on its face. And he was cross-examined at the time. And I think equally important is that much of his statement that was put to him, most of it, was accepted by the witness as being true. So the remaining parts that he is not sure of or that he cannot accept, would be admissible with those parts that he accepts at least to provide context. But it is the Prosecution's submission that the Defence, having opened the door to these statements from Mr. Janicevic, all of it should be received in evidence. May it please you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the Chamber's view, the statement should be received -- the testimony that's recorded in the transcript should be received in evidence as an exhibit. It does so because there can be no question as to the circumstances in which that evidence was given and that it was given under oath and as to who made it. To what extent, if any, the Chamber may have regard to the contents of that evidence or relevance to questions of fact and truth is something the Chamber will determine when it comes to consider the whole of the evidence. It is not necessarily or automatically the case because this evidence is now received that it would place any reliance on that transcript for issues of truth. I've said that to make it clear to you and to Mr. Djurdjic that you should not read too much into the reception of this transcript. Thank you. You are still standing, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to respond to Mr. Stamp. I have understood you, but I don't think Mr. Stamp's arguments hold water. We've had a number of statements we've quoted from the transcript here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Don't worry about his arguments, worry about our reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01555.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm moving to an entirely different topic, and I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must interrupt you then, I am afraid, Mr. Stamp, because there are other trial and other commitments by us continuing in the day. We must adjourn now to resume on Monday. We must ask you to remain over the weekend, and we continue on Monday. A Court Officer will give you further assistance when we adjourn. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 15th day of March, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
